tags.gist: Wants a GenAI device judged as a bounded clinical capability with defined scope, competencies, failure tolerances, supervision needs and continuous requalification.
Supports exploring the competency approach, since validation built on bounded inputs and exhaustive tests fits open-ended, evolving systems poorly.
Calls benchmarking plus confirmation a strong foundation and would extend it into a lifecycle where competence is bounded, stress-tested, profiled, monitored and requalified.
Says competence means operating safely within an envelope, recognizing limits, failing safely and escalating, and keeping those abilities over the lifecycle.
Proposes a sponsor-defined competency envelope of scope, operating and safety boundaries, reinforcing evaluation of the full deployed configuration.
Wants failure competence evaluated explicitly, recognize, refuse, escalate, recover, with safe recovery after tool failure a gating competency for agentic systems.
Wants the unit of evaluation moved to the interaction trajectory, with scenarios that progressively add contradictions, resistance and escalation across turns.
Wants trajectory tests paired with stress testing across normal, edge, adversarial and failure conditions as a repeatable method.
Cautions against one aggregate score; wants non-compensable minimum floors for safety-critical capabilities alongside overall thresholds.
Proposes a competency dependency graph mapping the capabilities each safety-critical function relies on, testing nodes and the integrated workflow.
Recommends a hybrid evidence model of public, sequestered and sponsor-specific benchmarks plus clinical confirmation, with public ones as shared vocabulary.
Proposes a standardized, versioned Clinical AI Competency Profile disclosing what was tested, under what conditions, with versions and limitations, not a single score.
Wants a foundation model capability profile kept distinct from the device competency profile, complementing master files while sponsors stay responsible.
Encourages academia, societies, health systems and labs to profile devices against standardized competencies, versioned and multidimensional rather than a leaderboard.
Wants benchmark suites as machine-executable regulatory assets, reusable for authorization, component changes and periodic requalification.
Proposes a configuration baseline at authorization and competency impact analysis so delta testing scales to which competencies a change could affect.
Treats competency as a lifecycle property with predefined risk-based requalification triggers, since guidelines, populations and tools change even when the device does not.
Concludes with four principles, bounded competence, knowing when not to act, executable longitudinal evidence and observable benchmarks, reframing the regulatory question.
